Check samples for duplicates, possible contamination and different ancestry

Source: R/rkn_check_samples.R
rkn_check_samples.Rd

Summarises, for each sample, its relatives and its mean kinship with the rest of the cohort, and flags three kinds of anomalies before a selection:

  • possible duplicates or monozygotic twins: pairs with a kinship of at least 0.354. They need no action for the selection, which keeps at most one of them, but they are worth a quality check;

  • possible contamination: samples related to unusually many others, with an unusually high kinship even with the samples they are not related to. A sample containing DNA from more than one person tends to appear slightly related to everyone, and can merge many families into one; excluding it (argument exclude of rkn_graph_from_kinship) restores the real families;

  • possible different ancestry: samples with an unusually low kinship with the samples they are not related to. The ancestry of an individual is the population their forebears come from; populations separated for many generations differ in the frequencies of genetic variants, and KING estimates are negative for pairs of individuals from different populations (Manichaikul et al., 2010). This flag is informative only: these samples are related to no one, so they change neither the network nor the selection, and they need not be excluded for it. It is reported because ancestry matters for some downstream analyses, such as association studies, where it is usually accounted for with the principal components of the genotypes (Price et al., 2006). A low mean kinship is only a hint: assessing ancestry requires the genotypes.

Nothing is removed: the decision is left to the user. rkn_graph_from_kinship runs this check by default (argument check) and summarises the duplicates and the contamination it finds in a warning.

Usage

rkn_check_samples(
  x,
  threshold,
  samples = NULL,
  z_kinship = 5,
  z_relatives = 3,
  z_relatives_only = 5,
  z_ancestry = -5
)

Arguments

x

Kinship estimates, either a square symmetric matrix with the sample identifiers as row and column names (the diagonal is ignored), or a data frame with one row per pair of samples, such as the .kin0 output of KING or the output of plink2 --make-king-table. In a data frame, the two identifier columns are recognised by the names ID1 and ID2 (KING), IID1 and IID2 (PLINK 2) or id1 and id2, and the kinship column by the name kinship, regardless of case.

threshold

The kinship coefficient from which two samples are considered related: a number, or one of "duplicate", "first", "second" and "third", which select the cutoff of KING for relatives of that degree or closer (see Details). There is no default: the choice depends on the study.

samples

Optional character vector with the identifiers of all genotyped samples, for instance the IID column of the PLINK .fam or .psam file. Pair tables usually list only related pairs, so samples without relatives appear in no row; samples adds them to the network as unrelated individuals. Ignored for a matrix.

z_kinship, z_relatives

A sample is flagged as possible contamination when the robust z-score of its mean kinship exceeds z_kinship and that of its number of relatives exceeds z_relatives.

z_relatives_only

When the mean kinship cannot be computed, a sample is flagged as possible contamination when the robust z-score of its number of relatives exceeds z_relatives_only.

z_ancestry

A sample is flagged as possible different ancestry when the robust z-score of its mean kinship is below z_ancestry.

Value

An object of class rkn_sample_check, with a print method: a list with elements

samples

a data frame with one row per sample: id; n_relatives, the number of samples with a kinship of at least threshold; n_duplicate, n_first, n_second and n_third, the relatives by degree; mean_kinship, the mean kinship with the samples it is not related to (see Details); the robust z-scores z_relatives and z_kinship; flag, "possible contamination", "possible different ancestry" or an empty string;

duplicates

a data frame of the pairs with a kinship of at least 0.354;

contamination

a data frame of the samples flagged as possible contamination, with largest_family_without, the size of the largest family of the network after removing the sample;

threshold, largest_family

the threshold used and the size of the largest family of the network;

largest_family_without_flagged

the size of the largest family after removing all the samples flagged as possible contamination together. When several contaminated samples are related to the same samples, removing one of them leaves the others holding the families together, so only the joint removal shows their effect. It equals largest_family when no sample is flagged;

mean_kinship_available

whether the mean kinship could be computed.

Details

The robust z-score of a value is its distance from the median of the cohort in units of the median absolute deviation (MAD), so that the anomalies being sought do not inflate the scale. When the MAD is zero, as for the number of relatives in a cohort where most samples have none, the mean absolute deviation from the median is used instead, rescaled to be comparable with the MAD. The number of relatives enters on the logarithmic scale, log(1 + relatives).

The mean kinship of a sample is computed over the samples it is not related to, that is over the pairs below the third-degree cutoff of KING (0.0442): true relatives raise the kinship of a few pairs only, whereas contamination raises it with everyone, so leaving the relatives out keeps a sample with many true relatives, or a member of a small cohort with one close relative, from looking anomalous. The mean therefore requires a kinship matrix or a pair table that lists every pair. With a table of related pairs only, it is not available: contamination is then judged on the number of relatives alone (see z_relatives_only) and ancestry is not assessed.

Relatives are counted by degree with the KING cutoffs listed in rkn_graph_from_kinship.

References

Manichaikul A, Mychaleckyj JC, Rich SS, Daly K, Sale M, Chen WM (2010). Robust relationship inference in genome-wide association studies. Bioinformatics, 26(22), 2867–2873. doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btq559

Price AL, Patterson NJ, Plenge RM, Weinblatt ME, Shadick NA, Reich D (2006). Principal components analysis corrects for stratification in genome-wide association studies. Nature Genetics, 38(8), 904–909. doi:10.1038/ng1847

See also

rkn_graph_from_kinship

Examples

# A synthetic cohort of 200 samples: 30 parent-child pairs, one sample genotyped
# twice (S199 and S200), one contaminated sample (S001), whose kinship is raised with
# everyone, and 15 samples of a different ancestry (S181 to S195).
set.seed(1)
ids <- sprintf("S%03d", 1:200)
K <- matrix(rnorm(200^2, -0.015, 0.004), 200, 200, dimnames = list(ids, ids))
K[upper.tri(K)] <- t(K)[upper.tri(K)]
ancestry <- 181:195
K[ancestry, -ancestry] <- rnorm(15 * 185, -0.15, 0.03)
K[-ancestry, ancestry] <- t(K[ancestry, -ancestry])
for (i in seq(2, 60, by = 2)) K[i, i + 1] <- K[i + 1, i] <- 0.25
K["S199", "S200"] <- K["S200", "S199"] <- 0.49
K["S001", -1] <- K[-1, "S001"] <- rnorm(199, 0.045, 0.01)
diag(K) <- 0.5

chk <- rkn_check_samples(K, threshold = "third")
chk
#> <rkn_sample_check> 200 samples, relatedness threshold 0.0442
#> 
#> Possible duplicates or monozygotic twins (kinship >= 0.354): 1 pair(s)
#>   id1  id2 kinship
#>  S199 S200    0.49
#> 
#> Possible contamination: 1 sample(s)
#> (related to unusually many samples,
#> with an unusually high kinship even with unrelated ones)
#>    id n_relatives mean_kinship z_relatives z_kinship largest_family_without
#>  S001         105       0.0364        10.2      81.5                      2
#> Largest family of the network: 121 samples;
#> without all the flagged samples together: 2 samples.
#> 
#> Possible different ancestry (mean kinship far below the cohort): 15 sample(s)
#> These do not affect the selection; see $samples for the values.
head(chk$samples)
#>     id n_relatives n_duplicate n_first n_second n_third mean_kinship
#> 1 S001         105           0       0        0     105   0.03636107
#> 2 S002           1           0       1        0       0  -0.02538556
#> 3 S003           2           0       1        0       1  -0.02546515
#> 4 S004           2           0       1        0       1  -0.02614858
#> 5 S005           1           0       1        0       0  -0.02548009
#> 6 S006           2           0       1        0       1  -0.02459609
#>   z_relatives  z_kinship                   flag
#> 1   10.152469 81.5466443 possible contamination
#> 2    0.000000 -0.3442226                       
#> 3    1.036818 -0.4497839                       
#> 4    1.036818 -1.3561702                       
#> 5    0.000000 -0.4695907                       
#> 6    1.036818  0.7028056                       

# Build the network without the possibly contaminated sample; the warning still
# reports the duplicates
g <- rkn_graph_from_kinship(K, threshold = "third", exclude = chk$contamination$id)
#> Warning: Sample check: 1 pair of possible duplicates or monozygotic twins. See rkn_check_samples() for details and the argument `exclude` to leave samples out; check = FALSE skips this check.
